drills.title: Medical Patient Assessment
drills.summary: Work a medical primary survey, focused history, vitals interpretation, and transport priority decision.
drills.protocolNote: General educational material for training. Confirm exact indications, doses, destinations, and documentation requirements with your local protocol and medical direction.
drills.seoDescription: Practice a structured EMT medical patient assessment with primary survey decisions, SAMPLE/OPQRST choices, and reassessment priorities.

content.introduction: This drill strengthens a repeatable medical assessment sequence you can use on almost any medical call.
objectives: Perform a logical primary survey order
Collect focused SAMPLE and OPQRST information

scenario.dispatch: 61-year-old with weakness and nausea at home.
scenario.scene: Private residence, no hazards, family present.
scenario.patient: Sitting on the couch, pale, speaking in full sentences, oriented.

instructions: Complete each interactive decision in order.
Treat this as general training—not a local protocol worksheet.
Pass requires correct critical actions and at least 70% on knowledge checks.

activities.title: Order the primary survey
activities.prompt: Put these medical assessment steps in a practical field order.

activities.title: Priority decision
activities.prompt: The patient remains pale with ongoing nausea. BP 88/54, HR 118, SpO2 94% on room air. What is the best immediate priority?

choices.text: Complete a full head-to-toe before any treatment
choices.feedback: Unstable perfusion findings should drive immediate support and rapid transport planning.

choices.text: Support ABCs, treat for shock per scope, and prepare for priority transport
choices.feedback: Hypotension, tachycardia, and poor color make this a high-priority medical patient.

choices.text: Wait for a 12-lead before any supportive care
choices.feedback: Diagnostics can wait behind immediate ABC and perfusion support.

activities.title: Assessment tools
activities.prompt: Select the tools most useful for the next focused assessment of this weak, pale adult.

criticalActions.text: Protect yourself and size up the scene before patient contact
Assess airway, breathing, and circulation early
Identify unstable vital-sign patterns and escalate priority
Reassess after interventions and during transport

knowledgeChecks.question: Which finding most strongly suggests a higher transport priority?
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Shock signs raise priority regardless of the eventual diagnosis.

knowledgeChecks.question: What should happen after oxygen or position changes?
options: Reassess mental status, breathing, and vitals
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Reassessment confirms whether the patient improved, stayed the same, or worsened.

completionCriteria: Scored at least 70% on knowledge checks

debrief.summary: Medical assessment is a sequence, not a checklist race.
takeaways: Primary survey comes before detailed history when findings are unstable.
Vitals change priority more than the working label.
commonMisses: Collecting a long history before ABCs
Ignoring hypotension because the patient is still talking

drills.title: Trauma Patient Assessment
drills.summary: Prioritize XABC trauma assessment, hemorrhage control timing, and rapid transport cues.
drills.protocolNote: General educational material for training. Confirm exact indications, doses, destinations, and documentation requirements with your local protocol and medical direction.
drills.seoDescription: Practice trauma patient assessment priorities including hemorrhage control, airway, breathing, circulation, and rapid transport decisions.

content.introduction: Trauma assessment fails when bleeding and airway threats are delayed by a detailed secondary survey.
objectives: Identify life threats that stop the survey
equipment: C-collar and packaging gear as locally indicated

scenario.dispatch: MVC, one patient, bleeding from a lower extremity.
scenario.scene: Stable vehicle, no fire, bystanders present.
scenario.patient: Responsive adult with arterial bleeding from the right lower leg and rapid breathing.

instructions: Select actions in clinical priority order.
Do not invent local spinal packaging rules—use general educational priorities.

activities.title: XABC order
activities.prompt: Order these trauma priorities for the bleeding extremity patient.

items.text: Open and protect the airway as needed
Assess remaining circulation and shock signs
Perform rapid trauma survey and package for transport

activities.title: Life-threat decision
activities.prompt: Bright red spurting blood continues despite direct pressure. Best next action?

choices.text: Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound and note the time
choices.feedback: Uncontrolled extremity arterial bleeding is a classic tourniquet indication in training scenarios.

choices.text: Complete a full SAMPLE history first
choices.feedback: History waits behind immediate hemorrhage control.

choices.text: Wait for ALS before any bleeding control
choices.feedback: BLS hemorrhage control should not wait.

activities.title: Transport branch
activities.prompt: After hemorrhage is controlled, the patient becomes pale and confused with a weak radial pulse. Choose the best path.

branches.text: Stay on scene for a complete secondary survey
branches.feedback: Shock with altered mentation after major trauma favors rapid transport after life threats are addressed.

branches.text: Limit scene interventions to life threats and begin priority transport
branches.feedback: Correct: treat threats, package, and move toward definitive care.

branches.text: Remove the tourniquet to reassess bleeding immediately
branches.feedback: Do not casually remove a tourniquet that is controlling life-threatening bleeding.

criticalActions.text: Protect airway and breathing after exsanguinating bleeding is addressed
Recognize shock and shorten scene time
Reassess bleeding control and mentation after interventions

knowledgeChecks.question: In XABC, what does the leading X emphasize?
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Massive bleeding can kill before a traditional ABC sequence finishes.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which finding supports rapid transport after life threats are managed?
options: Confusion, pallor, and weak pulses after major trauma
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Shock signs after significant trauma raise transport urgency.

takeaways: Bleed first when hemorrhage is massive.
Secondary survey is important but not first.
commonMisses: Lingering on scene with decompensating vitals

drills.title: Respiratory Distress Assessment
drills.summary: Differentiate distress from failure, choose oxygen/ventilation support, and reassess work of breathing.
drills.protocolNote: General educational material for training. Confirm exact indications, doses, destinations, and documentation requirements with your local protocol and medical direction.
drills.seoDescription: Interactive EMS drill for respiratory distress assessment, oxygen device selection, and failure recognition.

content.introduction: Respiratory calls are won by recognizing when a talking patient is about to stop ventilating effectively.

scenario.patient: 68-year-old upright, 2–3 word dyspnea, wheezes, becoming tired.

instructions: Choose support based on ventilation adequacy, not SpO2 alone.

activities.title: Interpret the picture
activities.prompt: Which pattern best matches impending respiratory failure?

choices.text: Mild distress only
choices.feedback: Fatigue, low rate, and drowsiness are failure warnings.

choices.text: Impending respiratory failure needing assisted ventilation
Anxiety attack without airway risk
choices.feedback: Objective fatigue and hypoxia argue against that.

activities.title: Support selection
activities.prompt: Patient is tiring with inadequate chest rise. Select appropriate immediate support tools.

options.label: Airway adjunct if no gag and indicated
Nasal cannula alone as sole support

activities.title: Reassessment
activities.prompt: After assisted ventilation, what reassessment matters most?

choices.text: Chest rise, mental status, rate/quality of breathing, SpO2/ETCO2 if available
choices.feedback: Reassessment must show whether ventilation improved.

choices.text: Only the patient's opinion
choices.feedback: Subjective report helps but is not enough.

choices.text: Nothing until hospital arrival

criticalActions.text: Identify fatigue and reduced air movement as failure warnings
Support ventilation when breathing becomes inadequate

knowledgeChecks.question: Which finding is the strongest failure clue?
options: Anxious but pink and speaking freely
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Fatigue and mentation changes often precede arrest.

debrief.summary: Treat the work of breathing, not a single number.
commonMisses: Leaving a tiring patient on a cannula

drills.title: Chest Pain / ACS Assessment
drills.summary: Assess suspected ACS, prioritize ABCs and aspirin/nitro safety concepts, and plan hospital notification.
drills.protocolNote: General educational material for training. Confirm exact indications, doses, destinations, and documentation requirements with your local protocol and medical direction. Medication eligibility is agency-specific.
drills.seoDescription: EMS chest pain and ACS assessment drill covering OPQRST, red flags, medication safety concepts, and notification priorities.

content.introduction: Chest pain assessment balances symptom details with continuous ABC and medication-safety checks.
objectives: Apply medication safety concepts without inventing local doses

scenario.patient: Diaphoretic, clutching chest, BP 148/90, HR 96, SpO2 97%.

instructions: Focus on assessment and safety checks. Exact drug authorization is local.

activities.title: Focused chest pain flow
activities.prompt: Order a practical chest-pain assessment flow.

items.text: Medication safety screen if considering aspirin/nitro

activities.title: Aspirin safety concept
activities.prompt: Before aspirin (when locally authorized), which question is most essential?

choices.text: Any aspirin allergy or active contraindications per protocol?
choices.feedback: Allergy and contraindication screening is a core safety step.

choices.text: Favorite hospital sports team?
Whether the patient has eaten salad today

activities.title: Nitro safety concept
activities.prompt: Which situation should block nitroglycerin until clarified with protocol/medical direction?

choices.text: Recent phosphodiesterase inhibitor use / hypotension risk per local rules
choices.feedback: These are classic high-risk nitro considerations.

choices.text: Patient drank water one hour ago
Patient owns a bicycle

criticalActions.text: Screen for medication contraindications before suggesting cardiac meds
Plan early hospital notification for suspected ACS

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is hospital notification valuable in suspected ACS?
options: It helps the receiving team prepare time-sensitive resources
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Early notification supports team readiness for ECG and reperfusion pathways.

debrief.summary: ACS care is assessment plus safety.

drills.title: Stroke Assessment
drills.summary: Perform a structured stroke assessment, capture last known well, and prioritize destination/notification thinking.
drills.protocolNote: General educational material for training. Confirm exact indications, doses, destinations, and documentation requirements with your local protocol and medical direction.
drills.seoDescription: Practice EMT stroke assessment including BE-FAST findings, last known well, and hospital notification priorities.

content.introduction: Stroke care depends on fast recognition and a reliable last-known-well time.

scenario.patient: Right arm drift, slurred speech, last seen normal 45 minutes ago.

instructions: Check glucose conceptually because hypoglycemia can mimic stroke.

activities.title: Stroke screen elements
activities.prompt: Mark the assessment elements you should capture now.

items.text: Facial symmetry / arm drift / speech changes

activities.title: Priority
activities.prompt: Best next priority after ABCs and stroke screen?

choices.text: Rapid transport/notification toward an appropriate stroke-capable facility per local plan
Delay transport for nonessential paperwork on scene
Wait to see if symptoms resolve for an hour
choices.feedback: Do not wait out possible stroke.

activities.title: Hospital notification elements
activities.prompt: Select the elements that belong in a concise stroke notification.

criticalActions.text: Consider glucose as a stroke mimic screen
Notify early and protect airway if secretions/vomit risk rises

knowledgeChecks.question: Why check glucose in suspected stroke?
options: It is required for billing only

debrief.summary: Stroke drills reward speed with structure.

drills.title: Hypoglycemia Management
drills.summary: Recognize hypoglycemia, decide on oral glucose vs advanced options conceptually, and reassess mentation.
drills.protocolNote: General educational material for training. Confirm exact indications, doses, destinations, and documentation requirements with your local protocol and medical direction. Exact glucose cutoffs and ALS meds are local/scope-specific.
drills.seoDescription: Interactive hypoglycemia drill for EMS providers covering recognition, airway safety, glucose decisions, and reassessment.

content.introduction: Altered mentation plus diabetes history should make glucose an early action, not an afterthought.

scenario.patient: Diaphoretic, confused, responds to voice, BGL 42 mg/dL.

instructions: Assume local authorization exists only as a training premise when a choice mentions oral glucose.

activities.title: Immediate priority
activities.prompt: Patient can follow commands and protect their airway. Best EMT-level concept?

choices.text: Give oral glucose if authorized and the patient can swallow safely
choices.feedback: Airway-protective patients may receive oral glucose when indicated and authorized.

choices.text: Force oral glucose into an unresponsive patient
Ignore glucose because BP is normal

activities.title: Airway branch
activities.prompt: The patient becomes poorly responsive with snoring respirations. Choose the next path.

branches.text: Open airway, suction as needed, support breathing, and escalate treatment per scope
Continue trying to pour oral glucose
Leave the patient flat and wait

activities.title: Reassessment timing concept
activities.prompt: After glucose administration, you should reassess mentation and BGL. Enter the minimum number of critical reassessment items from this list you will check: mentation, airway, BGL, vital signs.

criticalActions.text: Check glucose early in diabetic altered mentation
Confirm ability to swallow before oral glucose
Reassess mentation and glucose after treatment

knowledgeChecks.question: Oral glucose is inappropriate when:
options: The patient is awake and can swallow
The patient is unresponsive with an unprotected airway
The patient has a known diabetes history
BGL is low and mentation is improving with treatment

commonMisses: Oral glucose in an unprotected airway

drills.title: Anaphylaxis Recognition & Response
drills.summary: Recognize anaphylaxis, prioritize epinephrine conceptually, and support airway/breathing.
drills.protocolNote: General educational material for training. Confirm exact indications, doses, destinations, and documentation requirements with your local protocol and medical direction. Epinephrine dose/device authorization is local and scope-specific.
drills.seoDescription: EMS anaphylaxis drill covering recognition, epinephrine priority concepts, airway support, and reassessment.

content.introduction: Anaphylaxis is a multi-system emergency. Delaying epinephrine for minor tasks is a common training miss.
equipment: Antihistamine only if locally included after epinephrine priorities

scenario.patient: Urticaria, wheezing, swollen lips, BP 82/50, anxious.

instructions: Treat epinephrine as the priority concept when authorized—do not invent mg doses here.

activities.title: Recognition
activities.prompt: Why does this presentation meet anaphylaxis concern?

choices.text: Skin findings plus respiratory compromise and hypotension after exposure
Isolated itchy finger only
Chronic seasonal allergies alone

activities.title: Response order
activities.prompt: Order the educational response priorities.

items.text: Administer epinephrine if authorized and indicated
Reassess and prepare for possible repeat dosing per protocol

activities.title: Immediate gear
activities.prompt: Select immediate gear for this patient.

criticalActions.text: Reassess BP, work of breathing, and mentation

knowledgeChecks.question: Which medication concept comes first in true anaphylaxis when authorized?
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Epinephrine is the priority treatment concept.

debrief.summary: Anaphylaxis care is speed plus reassessment.

drills.seoDescription: Crew-oriented cardiac arrest drill for role assignment, CPR/AED sequencing, and team communication.

content.introduction: High-performance arrest care is role clarity under stress.
objectives: Assign compressor, AED, and airway/support roles

activities.title: First 60 seconds
activities.prompt: Order the immediate arrest actions.

items.text: Power on AED and apply pads
Clear and deliver shock if advised

activities.title: Role clarity
activities.prompt: With three providers, which role split is most coherent?

choices.text: Compressor, AED/monitor operator, airway/BVM support with planned switch
Everyone compresses at once
No one touches the AED until ALS arrives

activities.title: Closed-loop calls
activities.prompt: Select effective team communications.

knowledgeChecks.question: After an AED shock, what comes next?

drills.seoDescription: Evaluator checklist drill for BVM ventilation including seal, rate, adjunct selection, and reassessment.

content.introduction: BVM skill is best verified by an evaluator watching seal, volume, and rate—not by reading alone.
objectives: Ventilate at an appropriate educational rate

scenario.patient: Unresponsive, snoring, no gag reflex, weak pulse.

instructions: This is an evaluator-verified drill. An evaluator should observe the skill and check each item.
Responder Roadmap can later supply evaluator identity; for now enter evaluator name/ID if known.

activities.title: Equipment selection
activities.prompt: Select appropriate gear for this apneic adult with snoring and no gag.

activities.title: Evaluator verification
activities.prompt: Evaluator: verify each critical performance item.

criticalActions.text: Do not delay ventilation for nonessential tasks

debrief.summary: BVM quality is visible and measurable.

drills.title: Hemorrhage Control
drills.summary: Choose direct pressure, packing, or tourniquet pathways and reassess bleeding control.
drills.protocolNote: General educational material for training. Confirm exact indications, doses, destinations, and documentation requirements with your local protocol and medical direction.
drills.seoDescription: EMS hemorrhage control drill covering direct pressure, wound packing concepts, tourniquet decisions, and reassessment.

content.introduction: Bleeding control is a decision tree under time pressure.

scenario.patient: Alert adult, deep thigh wound with ongoing heavy bleeding.

instructions: Use general educational indications; department SOPs may add packaging details.

activities.title: Bleeding ladder
activities.prompt: Order a practical bleeding-control progression for an extremity wound.

items.text: Expose the wound and apply direct pressure
Escalate to tourniquet if bleeding remains life-threatening
Note time and reassess distal status/bleeding control

activities.title: Tourniquet decision
activities.prompt: Direct pressure fails and blood loss remains massive from the thigh. Best action?

choices.text: Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound and note the time
Remove gloves to improve dexterity
Walk the patient to look for a bandage in another building

activities.title: Reassessment
activities.prompt: Select reassessment actions after hemorrhage control.

drills.title: Radio Report
drills.summary: Build a concise radio report with unit ID, age/sex, chief complaint, findings, treatment, and ETA.
drills.protocolNote: General educational material for training. Confirm exact indications, doses, destinations, and documentation requirements with your local protocol and medical direction.
drills.seoDescription: Practice building a clear EMS radio report with essential handoff elements and concise wording.

content.introduction: A good radio report is short, ordered, and useful to the listener.
equipment: Radio or phone notification process used by your agency

scenario.patient: 64-year-old female, pressure pain, diaphoretic, BP 100/62, given aspirin per authorization, ETA 8 minutes.

instructions: Select report elements and assemble a concise transmission.

activities.title: Essential elements
activities.prompt: Select elements that belong in a standard hospital radio report.

activities.title: Build the report
activities.prompt: Write a concise radio report (2–4 sentences) including age/sex, complaint, key vitals, treatment, and ETA.

activities.title: Clarity check
activities.prompt: Which report is better?

choices.text: "Medic 3 en route with a 64-year-old female, chest pressure, BP 100/62, aspirin given, ETA 8 minutes."
"We have a patient who is not feeling great and stuff is going on, more later."
A 4-minute biography with no vitals or ETA

drills.title: PCR Narrative
drills.summary: Write a CHART-style narrative from a short call stem and hit required documentation elements.
drills.protocolNote: General educational material for training. Confirm exact indications, doses, destinations, and documentation requirements with your local protocol and medical direction.
drills.seoDescription: Practice writing an EMS PCR narrative with CHART structure, objective findings, and required clinical elements.

content.introduction: Documentation is part of patient care. A usable narrative is chronological, objective, and complete.

scenario.patient: 72-year-old with wheezes, SpO2 88% on room air, improved to 94% on oxygen, transported sitting upright.

instructions: Write only from the provided stem—do not invent allergies or meds.

activities.title: CHART order
activities.prompt: Order the CHART sections.

activities.title: Write the narrative
activities.prompt: Write a brief CHART-style narrative for this call. Include complaint, respiratory findings, SpO2 values, oxygen, response, and transport position.

activities.title: Objectivity
activities.prompt: Which sentence is more appropriate for a PCR?

choices.text: "Patient stated he could not catch his breath; wheezes noted bilaterally; SpO2 improved after oxygen."
"Patient was dramatic and probably overreacting."
"Everything seemed fine so details do not matter."

knowledgeChecks.question: A strong PCR narrative should:
options: Stay objective and support medical necessity
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Objective, complete documentation protects patients and providers.

debrief.summary: Write what you saw, did, and observed next.
takeaways: Response to treatment belongs in the record.
